epithet: Hafiz al-Ummah (The Preserver of the Ummah); Abu Hurairah (Father of the Kitten)
role: Greatest hadith narrator in Islamic history
Governor of Bahrain under Umar ibn al-Khattab
summary: Abu Hurairah (RA) is the single most prolific narrator of hadith in Islamic history, responsible for transmitting over 5,300 narrations from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Despite spending only three or four years in the constant company of the Prophet ﷺ after his late conversion, his extraordinary memory, his complete dedication to the Prophet's company, and his lifelong devotion to transmitting knowledge made him the primary source of vast portions of Islamic law and practice.
biography:
Abu Hurairah's given name is recorded variously in classical sources, with al-Dhahabi listing over thirty opinions in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' on his pre-Islamic name. The most commonly cited view is that his name was Abd al-Rahman ibn Sakhr al-Dawsi, though some classical scholars including al-Bukhari recorded his name as Umayr ibn Amir. He came from the Daws tribe of Yemen and was born around 599 CE. His kunya 'Abu Hurairah' — Father of the Kitten — was given to him by the Prophet ﷺ himself because he used to carry a small cat with him. (al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', Vol. 2; also noted in al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir)

He accepted Islam in 7 AH (628 CE) when his tribal chief Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi, who had been a Muslim since the Makkan period, returned to Yemen after the Battle of Khaybar and brought many of his tribe to Madinah to take the shahada before the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurairah was among those who came with Tufayl and accepted Islam. From that moment, he made the most consequential decision of his life: he would become one of the Ahl al-Suffah — the poor companions who lived in the mosque of Madinah with no fixed home or income, devoting all their time to the company of the Prophet ﷺ and learning from him.

This decision, born of poverty and faith rather than any other calculation, placed Abu Hurairah in proximity to the Prophet ﷺ at virtually every waking moment. Other major companions — Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali — had families, businesses, and responsibilities that took them away from the Prophet's immediate presence for significant parts of each day. Abu Hurairah had none of these encumbrances. He ate when the Prophet ﷺ fed the Ahl al-Suffah, and he sat with the Prophet whenever he sat, following him like a shadow. The Prophet ﷺ noticed this and was recorded as saying: 'The closest of people to me on the Day of Resurrection will be those who send the most salah upon me.' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi; similar in Sahih Ibn Khuzaymah)

Abu Hurairah reported that one day he went to the Prophet ﷺ and complained of his memory, saying that he learned much but retained little. The Prophet ﷺ told him to spread his garment on the ground, then made a motion with his hands as if pouring something into it, and told Abu Hurairah to fold it to his chest. From that day, Abu Hurairah said, he never forgot anything he heard from the Prophet ﷺ. (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Ilm — related through authentic chains)

The sheer volume of hadith Abu Hurairah transmitted — 5,374 in the major collections according to the count of Ibn Hazm and confirmed by later hadith scholars — was a subject of comment and scrutiny even during his own lifetime. Some of the senior Sahaba, including Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ali ibn Abi Talib, on occasion questioned specific narrations. Abu Hurairah consistently maintained the accuracy of his transmissions and challenged those who doubted to point to a contradiction. Classical hadith scholars, including Imam al-Bukhari and Imam Muslim, examined his narrations with great care and found them reliable; the vast majority of his narrations in the Sahihayn have been authenticated and accepted by the ummah's scholars across the centuries.

Abu Hurairah himself was aware of the scrutiny and spoke of it openly. He said: 'You claim that Abu Hurairah narrates too much from the Prophet. Allah is the witness between me and you. I was a poor man and I served the Prophet ﷺ to fill my stomach, while the Muhajirin were busy in the marketplaces and the Ansar were busy with their properties. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever spreads his garment until I finish my speech, then gathers it to himself, he will never forget anything I say." So I spread my robe, and by Him who sent the Prophet with the truth, I never forgot anything he said to me after that.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Ilm)

Beyond his role as a narrator, Abu Hurairah served the Muslim community in other capacities. He was appointed governor of Bahrain by Umar ibn al-Khattab, where he served for a period before Umar suspected financial irregularities. Umar summoned him and questioned him — the encounter is recorded in detail in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra — with Umar stating that he had been a governor and now owned property. Abu Hurairah explained that the wealth came from horses he had bred, gifts, and his personal income, not from public funds. Umar accepted his explanation but Abu Hurairah subsequently declined further administrative appointments, preferring to devote himself entirely to teaching hadith.

After the death of the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Hurairah spent his remaining decades in Madinah as the primary teacher of the next generation of scholars. The great Tabi'un — including Hammam ibn Munabbih (whose Sahifah Hammam ibn Munabbih is the earliest surviving written collection of hadith, drawn from Abu Hurairah's dictation), Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Salih al-Samman, and Ibn Sirin — all transmitted from him extensively. His circle of students was so large and so productive that the hadith of Abu Hurairah form a substantial portion of every major hadith collection.

He died in 57 AH (678 CE) at approximately 78 years of age in Madinah and was buried in al-Baqi. He reportedly said before his death: 'Do not make mourning for me, for I am going to meet someone I love — Muhammad ﷺ and his companions.' The Prophet ﷺ had said of those who transmitted knowledge: 'Whoever guides to goodness has the same reward as the one who does it.' Abu Hurairah, by transmitting the words and deeds of the Prophet ﷺ to generation after generation, earned a portion of the reward of every act of worship, every prayer, every fast, every legal judgment that was based on his narrations — a legacy that endures until the Day of Judgment.

key_events.event: Accepted Islam; traveled to Madinah with Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi; became one of the Ahl al-Suffah
The Prophet ﷺ gave him the miraculous gift of perfect memory by spreading his garment
Named 'Abu Hurairah' by the Prophet ﷺ because of his small cat
Accompanied the Prophet ﷺ on the Farewell Hajj and participated in the final year of his company
Appointed governor of Bahrain by Umar ibn al-Khattab
Present in Madinah during the fitna period; continued teaching hadith
Died in Madinah; buried in al-Baqi

notable_traits: Extraordinary memory — the greatest narrator of hadith in Islamic history
Complete self-sacrifice for the sake of knowledge — chose poverty and proximity to the Prophet over wealth and security
Honesty and intellectual courage — defended the accuracy of his narrations under persistent scrutiny
Deep personal love and grief for the Prophet ﷺ — said he could not recite certain chapters of Quran without being overcome
Humility in his scholarly role — consistently attributed his knowledge to the Prophet's gift, not personal ability

key_relationships.tribe: Daws of Yemen — introduced to Islam by Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi
key_relationships.mother: Accepted Islam after her son's persistent du'a to the Prophet ﷺ
